title: Rotate Array
statement: Given an integer array nums, rotate it to the right by k steps, where k is non-negative. Do it in place with O(1) extra space. Rotating right by one step means every element moves one position later and the last element wraps around to index 0.
realWorld: A fixed-size ring buffer of the last n samples stores its entries starting at an arbitrary offset; flushing it to disk oldest-first means rotating the physical array so the logical head lands at index 0. Log shippers and audio buffers do this every flush, on buffers too large to duplicate.

examples.explanation: The last three elements wrap to the front. Each element i ends at index (i + 3) mod 7.
The array splits after index 1; the two halves swap places. Notice the answer is the two halves reversed in sequence but internally intact — which is the clue to the trick.
k is larger than the array. Rotating by 2 is a no-op, so k = 3 is the same as k = 1.

constraints: 0 <= k <= 10^5, and k may exceed nums.length

bruteForce.idea: Rotate right by one step, k times: save the last element, shift everything one slot right, put the saved element at the front.
bruteForce.whySlow: Each single rotation touches all n elements to move each of them one slot, and then the next rotation picks the same n elements up and moves them one slot again. The element originally at index 0 is copied k separate times, through k - 1 intermediate positions nobody ever reads, to reach a destination that was known before the first copy: (0 + k) mod n. With n = k = 10^5 that is 10^10 writes to achieve 10^5 net displacements.

patternIdentification: A rotation is not a sequence of shifts, it is a relabelling: every element's final index is (i + k) mod n, and that is known before anything moves. Whenever each element's destination is a closed-form function of its index, look for a constant-space rearrangement — reversal, cyclic replacement, index arithmetic — rather than repeating a cheap operation k times. The specific insight here is that a rotation is the concatenation of two blocks in swapped order, and reversing the whole array puts those blocks in the right order with each block internally backwards; reversing each block then repairs it.

optimized.idea: Three reversals. Reverse the entire array: the last k elements are now at the front, but each of the two blocks is internally backwards. Reverse the first k elements to repair the wrapped block, then reverse the remaining n - k to repair the other. Reduce k modulo n first, because rotating by a full length changes nothing.
code: public static void rotate(int[] nums, int k) {
k %= n;                  // rotating by a whole length is a no-op; without this, k > n overruns
private static void reverse(int[] nums, int from, int to) {
// ONE step of the naive rotation, shown as what it really is:
for (int i = n - 1; i > 0; i--) nums[i] = nums[i - 1];  // shift every element one slot right
// taking the tail element out is the cheap half; putting it back costs n moves
// k steps x n moves = O(n * k) — which is what the three reversals replace

commonMistakes: Omitting k %= n: with nums.length = 3 and k = 7, reverse(nums, 0, 6) walks straight off the end and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. The test that catches it is always the one where k is bigger than the array, which is easy to leave out.

Reversing the two blocks first and the whole array last: the order is not symmetric. [1,2,3,4,5,6,7] with k = 3 then comes back [4,5,6,7,1,2,3], which is a rotation by 3 to the LEFT — it looks plausible and passes any test whose input is a palindrome.

Using cyclic replacement (follow index i to (i + k) % n, place, repeat) without counting the elements moved or stepping by gcd(n, k): with n = 6 and k = 2 the cycle visits only 0, 2, 4 and returns to the start, so the odd indices are never touched and half the array keeps its original values.
